summary:
Uşak is a province of Turkey, and trans visitors to Uşak stand under the national framework documented across the country. No province-specific trans-related source exists for Uşak, so the absence of a documented local ban or local incident is not evidence of permissiveness; the national pattern is the operative expectation.

Turkey's danger to trans visitors is structured and documented rather than residual prejudice. Kaos GL's 2025 review, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People," finds hostility toward LGBTI+ people converted into explicit state policy, with "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions, the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation for the first time in years, restrictions on expression and artistic freedom, and events cancelled or banned.

The same monitoring counted 313 liberty violations in 2025, roughly two and a half times the previous year's total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations (up from 51 the prior year), 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings in which trans people were the most affected, private-life violations rising from 16 to 67 including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy, and 61 travel bans.

A leaked omnibus draft, the "11th Judicial Package," reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, conditioned on mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison and patients up to three years, with possible pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns it would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest.

Street-level enforcement already operates as though such prohibitions were in force. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them.

Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, creating a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison, and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.
tangentialFactors:
The Erdoğan government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals," language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Under that framing the draft legislative package was before the government as of October 2025; its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Uşak province has no documented trans-specific incident, ban, or protection mechanism in the source inventory. The province's exposure is inherited from the national regime rather than generated locally, so a visitor's practical risk assessment should rest on the country-wide pattern of checkpoint stops, document checks, and detention decisions rather than on any Uşak-specific record.
localsOnly:
Residents of Uşak live under the same national legal and administrative framework as visitors, but with the additional exposure that comes from being documented residents rather than transient visitors: registered-address records, national identity documents, and residence in a jurisdiction where 299 detention decisions and 61 travel bans were recorded in 2025.

Trans residents seeking transition-related care face the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation, which barred hospitals from recording the "other" option on medical-board reports and required e-reports to be issued, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for such reports. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records.

The pending 11th Judicial Package would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, and would expose both providers and patients to criminal penalties. Residents have no province-level recourse documented in the inventory; opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised trans prisoner custody conditions in parliament on 12 December 2025, indicating that contestation occurs at the national level.
outOfScopeNotes:
No province-specific source for Uşak exists in the inventory. Whether Uşak police conduct GBT-style stops of trans people, whether local events are banned, or whether any local protection mechanism exists is unresolved and not sourced here; the national pattern is applied by inference from the country-wide framework.

The 11th Judicial Package was a leaked draft as of the October 2025 reporting and had not been passed at that time. Whether it has since been enacted, amended, or withdrawn is unresolved and not sourced in the inventory.

The inventory does not resolve whether the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation on medical-board reports applies uniformly across all provinces or has been subject to legal challenge. It also does not document the current operational status of any LGBT organisation in Uşak or whether the organisation closure reported by Kaos GL in 2025 was a national body or a provincial one.
